header.title: System Card
header.subtitle: A plain-language record of how an AI product works and how it’s checked.

stories.label: 01 · Agent Stories
stories.title: Each Agent Has One Job and Clear Limits
stories.intro: Every role is written like a user story.
stories.definition: An agent story is a user story adapted for an AI agent

agents.name: Planner
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when I talk through ideas, I want them turned into tasks.
may: Collect my notes
Write specs
Write one labeled instruction per agent
Keep the project record in repo
never: Touch the code
Send instructions while I’m still giving notes
Present a guess as a fact
decides: How to group notes into tasks
stops: The instruction is written and labeled for one agent
works: The builder needs no follow-up questions
The checklist that comes back matches what I asked for

agents.name: Coder
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when I hand over a task, I want it built, tested and live, so I can judge the result instead of supervising the work.
may: Read the spec and the project rules
Write code and course content
Run tests and audits
Push to the live site
never: Spend money or create accounts
Make anything public or delete data without me
Take facts from model memory
Swap in content before the judge’s review
Push without pulling and testing first
decides: Which checked sentences fit a lesson
stops: The batch is live with a Live / Not Done checklist, or a stop rule is reached

agents.name: Curator
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when a language starts, I want its content gathered from checked sources and arranged into lessons.
may: Choose the language’s official word list
Pull sentences from Tatoeba, recordings from Lingua Libre, and word facts from Wiktionary
Arrange words into lessons in a teachable order
Draft sentences where sources run thin, and mark them
never: Take definitions or verb forms from model memory
Push a course live or make it public
Touch a language another session is working on
Build a language on hold
decides: Which word list to use, and logs why
stops: The sources are gathered and arranged into lessons, or drafts pass 40% of a part.
works: Every word fact traces back to a source
Drafts stay under 40% of each part, and every one is marked
No word is tested before it’s shown

agents.name: Design System
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when screens repeat the same pieces, I want each one built once in a shared library, so every screen uses the same parts.
may: Move repeated pieces of the app into shared components
Give each component a page in the library showing its states
Show each component in desktop, iOS and Android styles
Keep the component list (COMPONENTS.md) current
never: Change how the app looks while moving a piece
Build a second copy of a component that already exists
Publish the library without me
decides: How each one adapts to iOS and Android
Which near-duplicates to merge, and which to flag for me
stops: The component is in the library and on the list, and the app looks the same.
works: The app’s styles are identical before and after

agents.name: Judge
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when a builder finishes work, I want an independent review, so the builder isn’t grading its own work.
may: Review every new sentence and screen
Give each sentence a verdict: Use, Reject, Keep, Fix or Cut
Rate each screen on nine design criteria
Check word facts against Wiktionary
never: Change code
Write outside the review folder
Claim to be a native speaker
decides: Whether a sentence is natural, correct and right for the learner’s level
What should replace a weak sentence
stops: The review is written, with a count for each verdict.
works: Every part is reviewed before it goes live
Each fix names the line, the correction and the reason
The audits stay clean after the fixes are applied

agents.name: Debugger
agents.story: As the orchestrator, when something breaks on a real device, I want a fresh session for the bug, so that the fix comes with the root cause and a test.
may: Reproduce the bug on a simulated iPhone and iPad
Read the code
Fix it
Add a test
never: Ship a guess
Fix more than its one bug
Touch another agent’s unfinished work
decides: Whether the bug can be reproduced
What only a real device can confirm
stops: The fix is live with its test, or it reports that the cause wasn’t found and what it needs from a real device
works: The new test fails without the fix

product.label: 02 · Product Definition
product.title: Who This Helps, Who It Doesn’t
product.intro: The intended users and uses, and where it isn’t the right tool.

columns.title: Where It Helps
items: Adults starting a European language from zero
Getting from reading to first conversations
Learners who stalled on gamified apps
Practicing for the official exam at your course’s level
Reaching a real CEFR level with an honest measure of progress
Self-directed study with no locks or streaks
Ten-minute daily lessons
Travel tasks: ordering, directions, forms

columns.title: Where It Might Help
items: Learners past the course’s level reviewing the basics
Classroom learners who want extra practice
Heritage speakers filling gaps in reading and writing
Listening at natural speed
Pronunciation (record and compare, never graded)
Spain’s Spanish (the course teaches Latin American Spanish)
Portugal’s Portuguese (the course teaches Brazilian Portuguese)

columns.title: Where It Hands Off
items: A native speaker’s ear: checked sentences, graded pronunciation, accent coaching (content is AI-reviewed, not yet native-checked)
Live conversation (tutors, language exchanges)
Children, and anyone who needs a teacher to set the pace
Certified proof of level (the official exams)
Learners who need games, streaks or rewards to stay motivated (Tamago has none, by design)
Other alphabets (Arabic, Greek, Asian languages) and professional language (legal, medical, business)

scope.label: 03 · Teaching Rules
scope.title: What Tamago Does, and What It Won’t

intro.text: Every lesson is written and checked in advance.
The AI runs only when you use AI chat, ask why an answer was wrong, or request extra practice.

scope.goal: Help adults reach a measurable level in a new language, with short form lessons, honest progress and no games.
scope.tableIntro: Each row picks the honest option over the shortcut most apps take.

rows.do: Wiktionary, Tatoeba and official word lists
Teaches asking to repeat, slow down or spell out
rows.avoid: Tapping a word for its translation

rows.do: A one-word verdict and the right answer
Honest numbers mapped to CEFR levels

groups.intro: Sent to the AI each time a learner chats, asks why an answer was wrong, or requests practice.

rows.does: Runs a short conversation at the learner’s level and answers the help phrases.
Picks the two or three most useful gentle corrections once the scene is over.
Notes on meaning, grammar and missing points. Not a score.
Explains one wrong answer in plain words.
Turns the learner’s request into practice that fits the question types.

evaluation.label: 05 · Evaluation
evaluation.title: How the Work Is Tested
evaluation.intro: The evaluation methods used across the AI industry, applied to Tamago’s own testing tools.

rows.artifact: Every lesson of every course, built and walked: 250,125 questions across nine courses
Nine craft criteria scored 1 to 5, from “no dead time” to “obvious in one second”
An independent model session reviews every sentence batch and screen. It changes no code, and a person has the final word
A verdict on every sentence (Use, Reject, Keep, Fix, Cut), each with a reason

Every new word is shown before it’s tested, across 24,435 lessons in nine courses. The exception is 152 words that look the same in English, like taxi and train. No lesson adds more than four new words.
Every fixed bug gets a test that fails without the fix. 51 test files
A script taps through a real lesson on a simulated iPhone and iPad before every push
A fast check before each push (about 30 seconds for an engine-only change, 6.5 minutes for a French content change), the full suite on GitHub after
Coverage of each course’s A1 word list (an official list where one exists, a frequency list where none does): from 79% to 97% across the nine courses

Conversations and explanations run on Haiku 5.5; practice generation runs on Opus 5.5. Each conversation stops at 14 learner turns, each device gets 5 conversations and 30 explanations a day (kept in the browser), and a monthly spend limit on the Tamago workspace is the backstop
A limit per signed-in learner, enforced on the server. Today the server has none; the device caps above can be cleared
Learner flags (“my answer should be accepted”) collected for review
Native speakers checking the drafted sentences
